utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before continuing with the evidence, there is one matter I wish to raise, and a matter with Mr. Ivetic. The trial support staff and the Chamber itself has gone to extraordinary lengths to resolve the difficulties you have encountered with translations, and yesterday we asked for confirmation that your own translator was now working full out on the translations and have regrettably received no reply to that. Mr. Ivetic, we would like that matter resolved today. We want to leave for the recess knowing that your translator is hard at work without obstacle. Are we going to get that assurance?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm in the process of preparing a draft correspondence answering the questions that were in the e-mail. I'm waiting to hear back specifics from Belgrade, but I can tell you our translator, as she has been doing, is hard at work and will be working on documents that have been rejected by CLSS and are in the process of being authorised by OLAD. We have enough documents already authorised by OLAD to keep her busy, and we should be getting in the next day or so other documents authorised by OLAD. So OLAD and I are work -- OLAD and the Defence team are working hand in hand to get all the documents for December that were rejected authorised for translation which should keep her busy, and CLSS is already booked -- working on the January bundle that we submitted to figure out which of those will be rejected which will then allow us to seek OLAD's assistance in having those translated by our translator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understood though that sufficient had been rejected for you to get confirmation that she could work throughout the period until we can come back without any interruption in the knowledge that she would be properly paid for it. Now is that not the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is the position, Your Honour. There are just additional documents that have yet formally been -- they have been rejected by CLSS but have not been identified with specificity for her -- OLAD to authorise, then they will be so specified I hope within the next day, and I'm sure that she will have plenty to work full time and even extra time during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hope that will be clarified this afternoon. I've found from bitter experience in this case that if we do not cross the T's and dot the I's on this issue, it will become complex again and counter-productive. So please bear in mind the urgency of getting this clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have been working full speed with both OLAD and with CLSS for these many month trying to get it clarified and doing things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you see this is the mistake you make going back over history --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm trying to draw a line under what has happened so far, I'm being positive, I'm looking at the situation as we stand here now. Please do not get back into history --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have not been going back in history. I have been trying to move forward and I will move forward, and in the time constraints of what time periods I have, I want a response for Your Honour. And our translator, be assured, will work as much as she is allowed and she works even beyond the 1000 hours, for we are only authorised with those hours, that's a separate issue, but we will exert all our resources as we have been doing to get translations completed, because CLSS does not have the capacity to do them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, our next is SD-1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case we require to draw down the screens until the witness enters the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. You are known to us as Witness SD-1. Are you able to hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Would you now please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The first stage of your evidence will be examination by Mr. Cepic on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let's first talk about your 16th of January, 2007, statement. Did you make a statement to one of the Defence investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sir, what about the 11th of December, meaning two days ago, did you not supplement your previous statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What about the answers you gave to the questions you were asked, were they faithfully recorded in both statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Indeed they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What about if you were to be asked the same questions today, would you still provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, we also need confirmation of the identity of the witness through the use of his pseudonym sheet, and then we can proceed with the details of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We just need one minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could I ask usher just to show to the witness this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, do you see your name on that piece of paper in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you identify the exhibit number for that document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first -- could we start with the statement before, and -- is it possible to have IC number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, to make this of value, there really needs to be added the date of birth of the witness and also normally the name of his father would be included. His name alone is insufficient for the purpose now. Now can you either add it or can it be returned to him to add it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I can do by myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the usher will return that to you to do that. Now, SD-1, are the details on that document accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that should now be handed to the court deputy. Would you give it an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC162, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, can you now identify for us the exhibit numbers for the statement and the supplementary information?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first statement is the number of first statement is 3D495, this is the statement from 11th -- actually, from 16th of January, 2007; and second one is from 11th December of 2007, and the number of the second one is 5D1380. And I would like to request for both statements to be under the seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I wonder if I actually have both of these. I have a document called a supplemental sheet dated the 11th of December -- yeah. So it is 5D1380; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we tendered the statement with the statement which is under the mentioned number. It is almost the same content but.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The statement is the statement not the supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have two documents here, maybe the court deputy can sort out the numbers for me, but there seems to be confusion in the way in which they were delivered. Can you identify which is which, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If I may clarify. I just received information that we sent the statement by e-mail, my assistant sent to all parties -- to all parties to relevant -- to all relevant subjects. This statement is after supplemental information sheet. And as I mentioned, content of that statement is almost the same as the content of the supplemental information sheet. And we just tendered -- we just would like to tender the statement, not the supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have to say I'm not at all clear what document -- I still don't know which is which. 5D1380, is that the statement that you're tendering?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. And I ignore then the supplemental information sheet. Very well. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we go -- Your Honour, with your leave, could we go to private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I have to mention some names, and if I mention those names we could disclose the identity of previous witness in this case and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, do you have anything to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 7 [Private session][Confidentiality partially lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I will touch briefly on paragraph 7 in which you say that Witness K-89 and -- that neither Witness K-89 nor anyone else from your unit could have torn up documents because the soldiers did not take documents from civilians and inspect them. Will you please tell me on what basis you make that assertion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry again, Mr. President, but I think that we have established here who the witness's commander was and other participants in his group, and therefore we could probably go back into open session for the substance of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, I'm some concerned about security for some witnesses, and especially if we by omission mention any name from that unit I think that will be a little bit unproper for security of both protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll continue in private session for the moment. If it turns out there was no damage done or there would have been no damage done by what is said, then we will simply make that evidence public at the conclusion of the evidence. So we will remain in private session just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have not received an answer to my previous question, so I will repeat it. On what basis do you say that your men could not have torn up documents belonging to civilians or even checked documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honour, I assert that my soldiers never had any contact with the civilian population and that they were never in a position to do that nor were they ever ordered to do so. I assert under full liability that they never checked the documents of civilians or tear up their documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, SD-1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You were asked by my learned friend that -- at least your answer to one of his questions was that it would not be case that your commander would address privates and it would go through you. And my question to you is: Surely you agree that there is a possibility that a battalion commander could and did, indeed, address his troops before an operation and even during an operation. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, I wouldn't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You are aware, I take it, that the members of the 3rd Army, that is, the army that is responsible for the Pristina Corps, themselves went down to the field and addressed troops within the Pristina Corps. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honours, to clarify, what does "to address" mean? Does it mean to have a conversation with a soldier, saying, for example, Son, how are you? Are things difficult? Or does it concern issuing tasks or assigning any kind of work on the ground? I think the two or not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My question simply is this, that a battalion commander can address his troops on the ground prior to an operation. If you don't agree with that, that's fine, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: I don't agree. He can't issue tasks to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: SD-1, in this context "address" means speaking to the men to give them moral encouragement, not give them specific tasks in the form of an order. Now, why could a battalion commander not do that to lift the spirits of his troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he could do that, yes, but only in the form of a conversation. As for my unit, I assert with full liability that in the course of carrying out combat actions the commander never had an opportunity to be with my men because he was in front of us with the units advancing before us. So I assert with full liability that the commander could not have spoken to my men in the course of the combat activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, actually, let's try and be precise here. I'm talking about prior to the commencement of combat activities. In other words, just before the combat group left your location, it's possible, is it not, that the commander could be addressing the troops, giving morale-boosting speeches to his troops. Isn't that possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: No, it's not possible because the night before that the air-strikes began, and you can imagine how frightened the men were. All measures of anti-aircraft defence were being taken. Movement could take place only along axis we regulated, and just before this activity the commander did not have any contact with my men. I assert that with full liability.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We find it impossible to make a judgement on this here in court at this moment, so we will redact the evidence that's been in this most recent public session and continue in private session for the moment, and then we'll review the position when we get to the end of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this question, and I'll come back to that issue later. Is it the case that you and your fellow soldiers viewed all Albanian men of military age to be legitimate targets; in other words, potential terrorists? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't hold that view nor did any of my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But you -- you're aware that other soldiers within the combat group had that view, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Not that I was aware of, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now, we started off by saying that -- or I started off asking you that the purpose of this operation was to destroy pockets of terrorists in the villages I mentioned. You agree with the basic purpose of the operation; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honours, we read out the tasks. We might as well read out the one from the brigade commander's order just in order to avoid any speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: SD-1, we can do that, but you were there on the ground; if I can't ask you, then who can I ask? It's really not a very controversial statement I'm putting to you. Your task along with the other members of the combat group was to destroy pockets of terrorism -- terrorists in those villages. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honours, my task was to lend support to the infantry component during the execution of this mission, and this request had been made by the battalion commander, or in this specific case the combat group commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Very well. And then this mission was to destroy pockets of terrorists in the villages that you went to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honours, yet again I wish to underline this. My task was at the request of the commander and upon orders by the commander to lend support to the infantry components. As for the overall task, this was something for the brigade command. My task was very specific and well-delineated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Should we understand then that you had no idea what you were doing there as a group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what was the group there to do, the combat group there to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was carrying out tasks, controlling that area around those villages. There were probably indicators showing that there was a terrorist presence in the area, that there were terrorists and their units present in the area, so we had probably been ordered to go there and complete this mission. But what I'm talking about specifically is my own task. I could not have known what the overall task was for the combat group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That seems very strange that you would not know what the overall task for the combat group was, but there we have it. Mr. Sachdeva, that's the limit of the witness's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So I take it from your answer that if there were indicators that there were no terrorists in village, there would be no need to go to that village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I just thought question was going in some different way and -- but it is not. I have no objection to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, it is up to the commander to say which axis will be taken for a certain operation. I didn't know at the time, nor is it my place to speculate right now, what would have happened if something else had happened and why anyone would have gone to another village if there were indicators that there was a terrorist presence in a certain village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm actually not putting a very difficult proposition to you. It's very simple. If there were no terrorists in a village, there was no need for the VJ forces or the police to go into the village. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: That is probably the case, but I can't say. This is a speculative question. I don't think it bears any relation to the specific task we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And that would have taken you roughly how long? Half an hour? One hour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a village. You don't take half an hour to drive through a village if there is no resistance. I can't remember specifically, but I think we took several minutes to drive through, perhaps up to ten minutes. What is being suggested here is quite arbitrary I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm basing the suggestion on the evidence of your -- actually, on the information from your commander. I take it you disagree. You spent 10, 15 minutes, is that right, through the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was a support unit. They walked through or marched through the village. They had to control -- to inspect every street, every street corner, every single house. Obviously whenever it was necessary - I don't really know this myself, I'm just giving you an example. I would have taken a different time from the infantry units. What I'm saying is that we drove through in trucks, in vehicles, and we simply drove through that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So the group in the front, as you say, searched every single street corner, every single house; that's right? The early hours of the morning they were searching all the houses in the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, what's your point?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may. I'm not sure what my learned friend is basing this assertion on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that's the objection, it's overruled. Mr. Visnjic, what is your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my objection is similar to Mr. Cepic's, I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's also overruled. The witness can deal with this question. It's an interpretation that was open to be put to him in light of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: SD-1, should I repeat the question or do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And what's your answer? Was every single house, every single street corner, were they searched by members of your combat group on the morning of 25th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was just a sentence that I used to give an example of how one passes through a village. There was an infantry unit going ahead of me, but I don't know what exactly they did there. They were quite quick passing through, and when the battalion commander ordered me to cross the village, I did so. We drove through the village in motor vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you use this as an example because that was your experience when you were with the VJ during the conflict, isn't it? That's what typically happened, forces of the VJ would go into Albanian villages and search the houses. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: (redacted) [Confidentiality lifted by later order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you give us an example of a place where the infantry ahead of you took a long time to pass through a village because of the job of searching? Just an example from your experience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is very difficult for me to come to grips with a question likely that. What exactly do you mean by taking a long time. How long do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it was you that chose to illustrate the difference between the time you would take in vehicles to go through a village and the time the infantry would take because of the different duties they had to search; and I want you to give me an example of the difference in time from your experience of an event that actually took place so that we can understand what -- exactly what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, they walked and they certainly took longer. I had waited up in front of the village before my commander ordered me to cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you can't give me another example of another occasion when the infantry took a lengthy time to pass through a village ahead of you because they were searching?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I didn't have that much experience with actions of that kind. I can't remember a single specific example therefore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution might then suggest that you must have been thinking of this occasion if you can't think of any other when you said: "They walked through or marched through the village, they had to control to inspect every street, every street corner, every single house." So was it this occasion that that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I just gave an example, a textbook example, if you like, of what happens when one passes through a village with some resistance or with no resistance at all, but I can't really cite any specific examples, I simply can't. I'm unable to cite a single one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We need to go into closed session now to enable you to leave the courtroom, so let's close the shutters, please. We now require to have a break which will last about 20 minutes. While we have that break, please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Unless, of course, my learned friend has an issue with the name of the village being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've already said that every name we mentioned and every time-frame we mentioned, in my humble opinion, makes it easy to conclude what unit and what individuals are being spoken about, and I still feel the same concern I expressed earlier, primarily because in this situation we have two protected witnesses and a clear order of this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's just get back into private session and let's get on with this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And as you said earlier, there was no firing from the village, and therefore I take it there was no combat activity in the village. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I said that I passed through the village and didn't see anyone. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying none of the property that you saw in the village was damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I passed along the road. I did not notice anything that might cause me to conclude that there had been any kind of torching or destruction there. I passed along that road. I was very much afraid for the safety of my soldiers. We had only two motor vehicles, and I think in such cases one's field of vision is narrower. But I don't think I saw anything that had been burnt from the point we entered the village to the point we exited from the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me ask the question again and please give me a simple answer. Are you saying none of the property that you saw in the village was damaged, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: SD-1, we -- this Court has heard evidence from people who lived in the village, eye-witness evidence, that the houses were torched, were burned, people were fleeing on the morning of the 25th of March, 1999. And I want to ask you: Is it your evidence that that didn't happen, that they're making that up? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't say that, nor am I saying it now. All I said was that along the road I passed along, I did not see any of what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, did you come to know about the destruction that was caused in that village, leaving aside whether you saw it? You must have heard that these things happened. You were there on the ground. This was your area of responsibility. You must have heard that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have responsibility only for a sector, not for a zone. The brigade command had responsibility for a zone. When I made a statement to a team in 2001, I learned that there were indicia that some things had happened down there, but then that morning when I passed through that village in the early morning hours, I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let's try and get back to my question. I didn't ask whether you saw it. I'm asking you, as someone who was in the village at some point in time on the morning of the 25th of March, did you hear from your fellow soldiers, from other sources, from the civilians that were in the village, did you hear -- did you find out that the village was being destroyed or was destroyed, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I just want to know that you kept yourself only on the road, and you didn't go here and there and -- even while on the road you didn't see any smoke or any -- you didn't smell anything which would show that something was burning? Or you kept your eyes always on the ground? I mean, that is something I would request you to answer, because if things are torching you would see the billowing, the smoke, and all that. So could you please elaborate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I passed through the village in the early morning hours. I did not see anything either burning or fire or smoke. I was looking straight ahead because I was sitting in my vehicle, in the front, I was looking at the road in front of me. I did not see anything.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honour, by your leave, I didn't say destruction. The Prosecutor said let's move on from the destruction. I did not hear anything about the killing mentioned here. I assert with full responsibility that at the time I heard nothing. I heard nothing in the course of the war. I only heard that there may have been victims a long time after the war in conversations with my colleagues, and I saw something about it in a book written by a lady. But I assert with full responsibility that at that time I neither heard nor saw anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I suspect you've probably answered this, but did you hear about any killings committed by the special police or the MUP detachment that was in the village?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this question. The witness has testified he saw no special police in the village, he saw nobody in the village, so I don't see the basis for this question by learned counsel. There was no such line of questioning in the direct, and I think we're seriously going beyond the scope of the direct examination at this point and are engaging in essentially a fishing expedition that might require additional cross-examination by other teams in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see nothing wrong with this question, it relates to what the witness had heard, and it may be answered. Can you answer the question, please. SD-1, could you answer that? Did you hear about any killings committed by special police or MUP detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness, I want to show you -- well, let me ask you this. You know that your commander kept a war diary, the command of the 2nd Battalion kept a war diary. You know about that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you know that that war diary contained reports of military activities on a daily basis from -- well, at least during the period that we're talking about from the 24th/23rd of March through to the end of the war. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And it's safe to assume that these reports were contemporaneous in nature, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honour, by your leave, I don't know when the commander wrote this, but he probably wrote such a report every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to show you one such report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we can have Exhibit PT -- sorry, 2019 on the screen, if we could go to page -- I believe it's page 3 of the Serbian version and page 3 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And, SD-1, what I'm going to do is show you an excerpt from the 25th of March. Now, the Serbian version is on the right-hand side at the top, and you'll see -- in capital letters you'll see two names. You see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see it says something, but I can't actually read it very well -- yes, now I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have the English for the 25th of March also, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, if it could be -- it's on the right page, it just needs to be scrolled down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the supplement at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Therefore, I suggest to you that this indicates that the village was cleansed of its civilian population.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it doesn't say that in the report nor can I say that. In the report it says something else, not that it was cleansed of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying this is what it says in the report; I'm saying to you that it indicates that the village was cleansed of its civilian population. If you agree, then you do; if you don't, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it doesn't mean what you're saying. This is military terminology. A commander cannot write a novel. He has to use just a single sentence. It would take too long to detail everything that had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But you tell me, what was there to cleanse in the village if there was no combat activity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honour, just the passage through the village might be called by someone cleansing of the village. How would they know there would be no fighting there, no combat?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm confused by that answer. Are you suggesting that the activity of passing through the village would be described as cleansing? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honour, when one passes through a village in combat disposition, that can be termed cleansing of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you've already mentioned that you gave a statement to the body for cooperation with the ICTY, and in that statement you didn't use the word "cleansing," you used the word "passing through the village." I suggest to you it's an absurd statement to say that if you were simply passing through the village, you would use the word "cleansing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what basis my learned friend is asserting all this. First of all, the document we see on the screen is not a document written or compiled by the witness or had contact with -- that the witness had contact with. We do not see the statement that our learned friend is referring to. Thank you. There are two point here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The -- there is no substance in the first point because the witness is clearly confident that he can deal with an interpretation of this passage. So far as the second point is concerned, what statement are you referring to, Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's a statement that's on my exhibit list which I believe the Defence should have. It is P3006, and it's a statement that he gave to the Commission for Cooperation with the ICTY. And that's the basis for my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. I see that document 3006 was announced, but I don't know when it was disclosed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you want me to indicate when it was disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you want me to indicate when the statement was disclosed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, there's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness, I don't know if you answered my last question before the deviation. My --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friends -- my colleagues are telling me that this exhibit cannot be opened in the system under that number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you released this exhibit, Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm advised, yes, Mr. President, and that's the exhibit number I have, and they indeed were disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you now open it, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: They were disclosed on the 31st of July, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleagues are now telling me that they managed to open it in the last few seconds, more than one colleague has said that, colleagues Ivetic, Visnjic, and Petrovic all say the same thing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what's your point?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to say that I have not had an opportunity of seeing that this document was in the system, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If having received notice from the Prosecution that they were going to use it and you were concerned about it, you would have tried to open it already and discovered that you couldn't. It would appear that you're only discovering that now, so let's get on with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness, I still require an answer from you, and essentially my question was that -- I'm putting to you that it is an absurd statement by yourself to suggest -- to say that the word -- essentially what you're saying is the word "passing" and "cleansing" are the same and they can be used interchangeably; that's an absurd statement, do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honour, by your leave, I didn't say that. It sounds even more absurd to me. I passed through there with my unit. In that statement you're mentioning, I was talking about myself. The commander was writing about the whole unit in his report, because he passed through the village with infantry. I marched through on vehicles. I simply passed through the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Very well. And therefore your commander in the infantry, as is indicated in this document, cleansed the village, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honour, the infantry passed through the village in combat formation without any resistance and without firing, and they left the village. In military jargon, this can be described as cleansing the village. It doesn't mean what the Prosecutor says it means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, whether your last point is correct or not - and there may be some argument about that, but perhaps not a great deal - it does seem on the face of it very strange if absolutely nothing has happened to then later write in the war diary that the villages were cleansed. Is that not rather odd unless something had to be done while they were going through the villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I assert what I said before was true. Battalion commander is not a lawyer, he can't take into account every single piece of phrasing. These circumstances under which this log was kept were difficult. Your interpretation is not correct. He had a different intention. He was trying to say something else when he wrote that. It is not what you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you should be aware that we've had a number of witnesses explain to us what cleansing means in this context, and no one so far has suggested it simply means going through a village in combat order. Now, do you want to say any more on the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't say that myself. I went through the village, but what they did can be called cleansing because they walked through the village on a house-to-house/street-corner-to-street-corner basis. How could they know that nobody would fire at them? If indeed no one fired at them, they would just get out and leave the village. In military speak, however, that can be termed"cleansing the village."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: SD-1, let me quote your answer to you. "The infantry passed through the village in combat disposition without any resistance and without firing and they left the village. In military jargon this can be described as cleansing the village." Now, that sounds to me like you describing cleansing as simply going through the village in combat disposition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can't take the liberty of commenting on those terms generally speaking. What I'm telling you is what actually happened and how I saw it, what the commander wanted to do, what he wanted to say. I'm not sure how I should launch into this story, but one thing is certain, it's certainly not what's being suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Witness, at this point in time I do not even know if whether you actually saw the infantry going through the village and how they went through the village. Do you want to try to clarify that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not see the infantry going through the village. They walked some way ahead of me. I said that I was waiting outside the village, waiting for my commander's order to go through the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. In the bigger picture, Mr. Sachdeva, I doubt if we've more time to explore this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May I ask one more question on this issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right -- yeah, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I have another witness lined up waiting to appear. I think my learned friend has already used up substantially more than the allotted time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think he's reached the allotted time, Mr. Cepic. He has an hour because this was a 92 ter witness, plus the equivalent time that you used in live evidence, which was 36 minutes. Please continue, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness, in an answer to the President you said: "I went through the village, but what they did can be called cleansing because they walked through the village on a house-to-house/street-corner-to-street-corner basis," that's what you said, and therefore earlier on when we were in a discussion about what took place in the village, this is the example you were referring to, isn't it, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is an argument. We've had all the evidence on this. Move to something else, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How many men were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I recall correctly, 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain in technical terms how much time you need to take up a position to set up an observation point and undertake all the other activities involved in relocating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: Your Honours, quite a lot of time. These are activities that require a lot of time and good training. Depending on the training, the time can vary, but not much. I need at least 20 minutes only to put the mortars down on to the ground. As for establishing the observation point and everything else, I need far more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of the war, were you able to inspect the battalion's war diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SD-1
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, the war diary that was shown here is something I saw quite a bit of time after the war, when I was making the statements I mentioned in the course of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. SD-1. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Witness, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming here to give it. You may now leave the courtroom, but just stay there for a moment until we bring down the curtains for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, your next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness is Lieutenant-Colonel Vladimir Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading that document aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Cepic on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant-Colonel, good evening.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: For the record, please give us your name.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Vladimir Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when and where you were born?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd of December, 1967, in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me what duties you performed during your military career?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from platoon and company leader, just through the technical service, chief of the service in the regiment and the brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down, this is impossible to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marinkovic, everything you say has to be translated, that means that you need to speak a little more slowly than you would otherwise do. So I wonder if you could deal with that question again. You said that you had been chief of the service in the regiment and the brigade, could you continue from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I was desk officer in the security department of the Pristina Corps, a desk officer in the security administration of the General Staff of the Army of Serbia and Montenegro, and now I am a trainer in the training centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, what schools have you completed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: After primary school, I completed the military secondary school, the military academy for the ground forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. This is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: There is no statement, Your Honour, for this witness. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ah, sorry, wrong Marinkovic. Sorry. My mistake. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: They are not cousins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lieutenant-Colonel, what schools have you completed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: After primary school I completed the military secondary school, then the military academy for the ground forces, communications stream, and then further training for command and staff, and then I took a course in the security and intelligence training centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is your rank now?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999, what duties did you perform?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998, on the 2nd of March, I was sent to the 52nd Brigade of the anti-aircraft defence in the Djakovica garrison, where I performed the duty of chief of security -- excuse me, chief of the security organ in the brigade command, until the 1st of July, 1998. On the 1st of July, 1998, until the end of the war, I was the chief of security in the 15th Armoured Brigade of the Pristina garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Djakovica previously. In that period, the period of your work in Djakovica, did you visit the Pristina Corps forward command post?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the escalation of the security situation in the area, not only did I visit the Pristina Corps forward command post, but I was also designated by the chief of the security department of the Pristina Corps to perform duties from the purview of the security organ at the forward command post of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the security situation was like at that point in time, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The security situation in that period deteriorated day by day, especially in the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: We had frequent illegal border crossings from Albania by persons who were illegally carrying weapons and equipment, and there were even conflicts with the border organs who were attempting to prevent them in their illegal crossings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that period, did you exchange information with the state security department?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And what was this cooperation reflected in?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I was designated by the chief of the security department and authorised by him to exchange information concerning terrorist activities in the area with the chief of the state security department in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The information that was exchanged was something I passed on to my superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, you mentioned the escalation of terrorism, especially at the state border. Will you tell me, in the depth of the territory were there any drastic incidents, what was the situation there like in the period we are talking about, 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In the depth of the territory, movements were observed of persons who were armed and in uniform. Furthermore, there were attacks on the civilian population, the MUP organs. The worst incident -- well, there were also abductions. The worst incident in that period was an abduction that took place in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: A person called Genov Stamen or Stamen Genov who was a sergeant first class -- or a sergeant, he was on leave and he used the regular line from Djakovica to Pristina which went through Prizren and the Dulje pass. I think that in the vicinity of the village of Stimlje, the bus was stopped by a group of armed members of the KLA. They entered the bus, they inspected people's identity papers, and they pulled Genov and some civilians from the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was Genov later found?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was buried in 2005. His body was found at a later date. He had been killed, and to the best of my knowledge, according to the forensic information, he had been tortured and slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We've already heard quite a lot about the activities of the terrorist forces. Did you have any operative information that there were women in the KLA ranks who in 1998 participated in the fighting directly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: While gathering information about the terrorists, we obtained various types of material. We saw pictures and videotapes, video footage, of women in uniform with KLA insignia. Later on, in 1998, when I was already in the 15th Armoured Brigade, in the general area of Komorane, a tank of mine was hit and those who knew about this, the tank crew, told me it had been hit from an Armbrust. Later on we investigated that fire and learned that the projectile had been fired by a woman. We knew what her pseudonym was, although it escapes me at the moment, her pseudonym or nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, in the course of this escalation of terrorism, was there resistance from villagers who didn't want to join the terrorist ranks?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean resistance to the terrorists by the local population?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Our information shows that there was resistance by the local population. I was a witness in the village of Glodjane where the local inhabits welcomed us. They told us there were no KLA members in their village, that we should not be afraid, that fire would not be opened on us, and that they didn't want to join in those activities. Also, there were examples of terrorists trying to take up positions in front of certain villages and provoke activity by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: On what basis, Lieutenant-Colonel, did you have that information? Did you personally enter the KLA bases?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: On completion of anti-terrorist actions, I did enter places where KLA members were based, and there we found various materials which they had left behind. From those materials, we drew conclusions about their activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, could you tell us what was this material because material can be anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We found remains of combat equipment, for example, empty cases for ammunition; weapons which they had not taken with them; lists of KLA members in a certain area, unit, or staff; various certificates that KLA members issued to the locals, such as certificates on recruited property or requisitioned property; then certificates on their military oath that they had taken, certificates allowing them to move through KLA-controlled territory, and similar materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I continue, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there an obligation for the local inhabitants to give money to the KLA if they were living in areas under KLA control?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we found certificates, or rather, receipts for money that the KLA had received from local villagers. I don't know in what way these villagers gave that money, but such certificates were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, did you find equipment used for torture?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in more than one location we found certain objects which indicated that they has been used for torture. In the village of Krusevac, in the course of the anti-terrorist action in 1998, in the courtyard in front of an improvised hospital of the KLA there was a device. I can describe as a bed where at one end there was a spike and there were two places in the shape of feet on the opposite side of the spike, and then there was screws or winches which could be turned when a person's feet were placed in those feet-shaped parts and then the head would be pressed against the spike.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you give me any other examples?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1999 in the area of Ostrozub we found bloody baseball bats and in other places likewise we found such things, although I can't remember every detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, could we go to private session? I just have one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We spent some time there in private session because the evidence which we heard could have given rise to a risk to an individual, and we're now back in open session and shall continue with the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Lieutenant-Colonel, I'm about to move on to a different subject. What exactly was your duty within the 15th Armoured Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: My duty was chief of the security organ, and this post was attached to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You're not a troop officer, are you, but can you please tell me in very rough terms what the area of responsibility was of the 15th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The area of responsibility was in central Kosovo, or rather, in the north of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the OSCE mission, did you have any contacts with them during their mission in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I want to know specifically about the situation in the Podujevo area late in 1998 and early 1999, what was it like?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In late 1998/early 1999, the situation escalated, or rather, the security situation was under threat throughout the area. Information reached us about the expulsion of non-Albanians from the Podujevo area, the area of Podujevo municipality. Likewise, terrorist forces had been observed along the entire Pristina-Podujevo road, I'm referring here to the main road obviously leading from Podujevo to Tenevdolski Tesnac [phoen] to the west. They dug-in there. They were fortifying their positions, digging trenches, and building roads. Even while looking from the road it was quite clear that they were armed. At the time there were kidnappings of people in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, the area around Batlava airport has been referred to time and again in this trial. Can you tell us what this was about? Was the army using this area to conduct drills?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's near the village of Batlava and this was an area that the army was using as some sort of a training ground for military drills at higher-level -- at a higher level of training.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long ago the use of that training-ground dates back to?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: When I took up my duties in the brigade, I was familiarised with all the training-grounds used by the brigade, including the one at Batlava.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you've mentioned this road -- now that I mentioned it in my previous question, did you perhaps come under attack along that road at any point?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Over a ten-day period, I twice had a close brush with the terrorists just along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 5D95, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you see this report in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have count 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you submit information for a report like this, a report concerning the situation that prevailed in the area?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but as far as I can tell it wasn't just me, other officials did that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 3D1035, please. 3D1035, please. Could we have count 3, please, 3.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, if you look at this, is this a description of the attack that you were subjected to, 3.1, that's what I'm talking about. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a description of the attack that took place on 24th of December. I was attacked on my way back from Podujevo to Pristina, I was on a mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sir, as the war encroached, did the sheer intensity of violence and terrorist activity keep on increasing?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was becoming more and more intense. I told you that over a ten-day period I had two such things happen to me. This is one situation, and then ten days later on the 5th of January in the Glavnik village sector, along that same road, the same sort of thing happened. I had a brush with KLA members. Should I describe that for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you want us to go into private session for this? Just in the briefest possible terms, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think there's any need for that. I'll try to stay brief. With me in the vehicle were two journalists. I was on my way back from Podujevo, and I was the one driving the vehicle. They asked me to pull over in the Glavnik village sector so that they could take pictures of the trenches along the road. I'm talking about the Podujevo-Pristina road. Once they were done taking photographs and we're now back in the vehicle, a car came out of nowhere and blocked our way, a Golf. Two persons emerged from the car, they were both wearing civilian jackets. Underneath their jackets we could see that they were wearing bullet-proof vests. Their hands were in their pockets, but you could see that they were grabbing something with their fists inside those pockets. One of them spoke up in Serbian, and he talked to the journalist who was on the back seat, right behind the passenger seat. The journalist falsely introduced himself as someone who worked for a Slovene TV station, that probably being the first thing that occurred to him at the time, and this person requested to see a Kosovo government permission to film the area or to take pictures of the area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you seriously want all this detail of this individual incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we haven't got to what matters, have we? Presumably something happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: And then I told them in Albanian, since I speak Albanian, that these people were all right, they were our guys, so we drove off soon after, leaving them quite baffled. We managed to save our necks, that was the bottom line.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you perhaps know from other sources that they checked passing traffic in a bid to assert their sovereignty throughout the area?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the whole area and off the main roads as well they had check-points, KLA check-points. This applied to all access roads to all of the villages in the area as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, we are now coming to the 24th of March. What about all the combat units of the 15th Armoured Brigade, did they not all leave Pristina on that day in the barracks this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of its combat units left the Pristina barracks on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: There is something else I would like to ask you as well. You weren't one of the troops. What about throughout 1998 and 1999, were you ever at the command post as an action was being executed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, several times as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever at the joint command post?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you describe it for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Probably is better translation if we see page 87, line 19, combined command post than the joint command post, but ... Can I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can and we'll have CLSS provide for us the document setting out the B/C/S and the English again in relation to that passage --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- from line 15 to line 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what this joint or combined command post was like?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: This joint or combined command post is something that was set up during anti-terrorist actions when units from my brigade would lend support to forces of the MUP during an action. Normally it was set up at an observation post or a battalion command post or a combat group command post, depending on what the unit was that was actually lending support, depending also on their whereabouts, on the whereabouts of the unit commander from my unit who was involved in the action and the commander of the MUP unit carrying out this anti-terrorist action.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were there other officers there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the two commanders, there were other officers there whose presence was indispensable for the work of the joint or combined command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: From both these bodies, the military and the MUP, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from both.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What's your military specialty, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a signalsman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, when it's convenient, find a place to interrupt the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just one question with your leave and I will finish. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Lieutenant-Colonel, what sort of communication equipment was used during those actions, concerted action, or support to MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The army used its own equipment that it had under the establishment, and the MUP did the same thing. It depended on the nature of the action being executed. For the most part, it was radio equipment. Needless to say, the army would use its own frequencies and the MUP would use its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let me just try to clarify this. Was there a unified communications system in place or not?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no unified communications system. We used a communications plan, the army did; and the MUP people probably had their own plans. Any sort of communication from either of these sources would normally end up at the joint or combined command post, but there were two separate lines of communication, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Marinkovic, we have to interrupt the proceedings for the day at this stage. You'll require to return tomorrow to complete your evidence; that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Meanwhile, overnight you must avoid any discussion with any person about any of the evidence in this case. Talk about whatever you like with whoever you like as long as there is absolutely no discussion at all about the evidence. Please now leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will see you again at 9.00 tomorrow in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one matter I wish to draw to your attention, Mr. Cepic, and that of Mr. Bakrac. Today you've reached a fairly significant point in the presentation of your case. You now have less than 20 hours of the time allocated remaining, and you still have a very large number of witnesses proposed. And I think so far we've seen an attempt in only two instances to seriously use other available means of presenting evidence, apart from oral evidence in court. You must, if you intend to lead the evidence of these witnesses, take a very hard look at how you're going to do that. Use the other means that are available to you or at least consider that. You have a break coming up when, no doubt, work can be done on that, but it's a matter of concern to us that you have reached this stage and have used only a -- less than half of the -- or led less than half of the witnesses, significantly less than half of the witnesses you propose. So until 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 14th day of December, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
